notes: Hand-written reference sheet. The accuracy and coverage judges grade the lesson against this, so 'accurate' means 'consistent with a source we control', not 'whatever the judge model believes'.

must_cover.point: What a large language model (LLM) is, in simple terms, and its limits: it only knows what was in its training data up to a cutoff date, it does not know private or very recent information, and it can confidently make things up (hallucinate).
A plain definition of RAG that explains all three words: Retrieval (find relevant information), Augmented (add that information to the question/prompt), Generation (the LLM writes the answer).
Why RAG matters: answers can use up-to-date or private information, fewer made-up answers, answers can point to their sources, and knowledge can be updated without retraining the model.

The preparation (indexing) step: documents are collected, split into small pieces (chunks), and stored in a searchable form. At a simple level, chunks are turned into embeddings (numbers that capture meaning) so similar text can be found.
The retrieval step: when a question comes in, the system searches the stored chunks and picks the few most relevant ones.
The augmentation step: the retrieved chunks are added to the prompt together with the user's question (and an instruction to use them).
The generation step: the LLM writes the answer using the provided information.
Limits: if retrieval finds the wrong or missing information, the answer can still be wrong. RAG reduces made-up answers but does not remove them completely.
At least one realistic use case (for example: a college helpdesk bot answering from the college rulebook, or a company support bot answering from product manuals).

facts: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a very large amount of text to predict and generate language.
An LLM's built-in knowledge is fixed at training time (a 'knowledge cutoff'); it does not automatically know events after that date or an organisation's private documents.
LLMs can produce fluent but false statements; this is commonly called hallucination.
RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. The term was introduced in a 2020 research paper by Lewis et al. (Facebook AI Research).
In RAG, relevant information is retrieved from an external knowledge source at the time of the question and added to the model's input (the prompt).
RAG does not change the model's weights. There is no retraining; the knowledge lives in the documents, and updating the documents updates what the system can answer.
Typical indexing: collect documents, split them into chunks, convert each chunk into an embedding (a list of numbers representing its meaning), and store them in a vector index or vector database.

Typical query flow: convert the question into an embedding, find the chunks with the most similar embeddings (similarity search), take the top few, place them in the prompt with the question, and let the LLM generate the answer.
Retrieval can also use keyword search, or a mix of keyword and vector search (hybrid search). A vector database is common but not strictly required.
Models can only read a limited amount of text at once (the context window), which is one reason RAG retrieves only the most relevant pieces instead of pasting every document.
RAG can let answers cite or link to the source documents they used.
Fine-tuning is different: it continues training the model and changes its weights. RAG and fine-tuning can be combined.
RAG reduces hallucination but does not eliminate it; answer quality depends heavily on retrieval quality.

misconceptions.wrong: RAG retrains or fine-tunes the model on your documents.
misconceptions.right: RAG adds retrieved text to the prompt at question time; the model itself is not changed.

misconceptions.wrong: After RAG, the model permanently remembers the documents.
misconceptions.right: Retrieved text is only part of that one prompt; it is not stored inside the model.

misconceptions.wrong: RAG guarantees correct answers / completely removes hallucinations.
misconceptions.right: RAG reduces made-up answers, but wrong or missing retrieval can still lead to wrong answers.

misconceptions.wrong: In RAG, the LLM itself searches the internet on its own.
misconceptions.right: A separate retrieval step searches a chosen knowledge source (which may or may not be the web) and passes results to the LLM.

misconceptions.wrong: Embeddings store the exact words or are the final answer.
misconceptions.right: Embeddings are lists of numbers that represent meaning; they are used to find similar text, not to answer directly.

misconceptions.wrong: RAG always needs a vector database.
misconceptions.right: Vector search is common, but keyword or hybrid search also works.

misconceptions.wrong: The whole document collection is sent to the model every time.
misconceptions.right: Only the few most relevant chunks are sent, partly because of the context window limit.
